task: Check two existing cards, written from PMC author manuscripts, against the versions of record saved on 26 November 2026. Give the printed page for every anchor and record every point of disagreement. The cards themselves were not edited.

sources_read.note: Version of record, Psychopharmacology 207(1):73-83, published online 13 August 2009. All 11 printed pages read, including Tables 1 to 4, all figure legends, the acknowledgements and the disclosure line. PDF page 1 is printed page 73, so printed page = PDF page + 72. Figures 1 to 4 are images; no values were read from them.

Version of record, Drug and Alcohol Dependence 115(1-2):120-130. All 11 printed pages read, including Tables 1 to 4, the role-of-funding, contributors, conflict-of-interest and appendix statements. PDF page 1 is printed page 120, so printed page = PDF page + 119. Figures 1 and 2 (survival curves) are images; no values were read from them. The supplementary tables named in Appendix A were not among the files.

summary.sc_bedi_2009: Every anchor is in the right place in the version of record and every number checks out, including the three that the abstract overstates. Six disagreements remain, all of them field-level rather than anchor-level, and five were already logged by reader 709 in 2026-11-15 as 'not yet in the card'. The most consequential is that two fields still call the effects table Table 2; in the published article it is Table 3 (p. 78).
summary.sc_lopez_quintero_2011: Every anchor is in the right place and every number checks out; the card's six reporting issues are all confirmed on the printed pages, and two of them can be stated more strongly. One field is now wrong: the version of record reports funding, authors' contributions and conflicts of interest on p. 128, which the card and its last reporting issue say are absent from the version read.

checks.anchor: key_findings[0] (design: 9 volunteers, three sessions, ascending doses, abstinence rules)
checks.note: Participants and Protocol are on p. 74 and run onto p. 75. Confirmed there: nine healthy right-handed volunteers aged 18 to 29 reporting ecstasy use at least twice; recruitment by online advertisements and word of mouth; three-session within-participants double-blind design; 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order with randomised placebo; sessions at least 6 days apart; sessions began at noon; at least 4.5 hours in hospital (p. 75); abstinence from cannabis 7 days, alcohol 24 hours, other recreational drugs 48 hours, checked by urine, saliva and breath tests.

checks.anchor: key_findings[1] (sample: 7 men, 2 women, age 24.0 (3.2), lifetime ecstasy 2 to 300)
checks.note: Results 1st paragraph and Tables 1 and 2 are all on p. 77. Confirmed: mean age 24.0 (SD 3.2); two of nine female; six identified as Caucasian; Table 1 gives lifetime ecstasy 63.89 (94.92), range 2 to 300, age of first use 17.44 (1.94), months since use 10.22 (9.15), past-year use yes n=4, no n=5; five reported daily cigarettes, five cannabis at least once, eight alcohol in the past month; Table 2 shows all nine had used cannabis, eight stimulants, seven hallucinogens.

Text on p. 77, Table 3 on p. 78. Every value confirmed in Table 3, together with the standard deviations as printed (19.0, 13.5, 11.6; 11.0, 16.2, 19.9; 5.0, 4.6, 4.0), diastolic 3.6 / 15.8 / 26.0 with F 8.0, and the statement that there were no serious adverse effects (p. 77).

checks.anchor: key_findings[3] ('sociable' -6.3 / -9.5 / +19.7; drug-by-time F(8,64) 3.1; t(8) 2.5, p=.04; t(8) 3.8, p<.01; POMS friendliness F(2,16) 1.3)
checks.note: All confirmed in Table 3 (p. 78) and the Results text (p. 77), including the printed 'p=0.04' beside the placebo contrast and the footnote setting the post hoc threshold at p<0.01. Editors' check of the degrees of freedom: the sociability interaction F(8,64) fits 3 drug conditions by 5 post-baseline times in 9 people, and the friendliness F(2,16) fits 3 conditions by 2 post-baseline times; both are internally consistent.

checks.anchor: key_findings[4] (imaging: amygdala corrected p=.052; ventral striatum corrected p<.05; visual and motor cortex; rating accuracy and speed)
checks.note: Confirmed: the three-way rating task with a button box on p. 75; left amygdala F(2,16)=9.64, p<0.005, PBO greater than 1.5 mg/kg t(8)=4.41, p<0.005, significant at p=0.052 after small-volume correction, no effect for fearful faces, right ventral striatum F(2,16)=9.75 with t(8)=6.13, p<0.001 at 0.75 mg/kg and t(8)=2.72 not surviving correction at 1.5 mg/kg, all on p. 77; the falls in V1 and M1 during the motor-visual task on p. 78; accuracy 0.89 / 0.91 / 0.86 (F 0.9) and reaction time (F 3.1) in Table 3, p. 78; Figures 3 and 4 on p. 79.

checks.anchor: key_findings[5] (limitations stated by the authors)
checks.note: Confirmed on p. 81 (preliminary; small sample; analyses restricted to two a priori regions; possible effects of MDMA on cerebral blood flow, with the Gamma et al. 2000 positron-emission study cited; all volunteers had prior exposure, varying widely; no correlation of brain signal with lifetime use or recency; ascending dose order for safety; 6-day minimum) and p. 82 (average 10.72 days apart; no session-order effect; no plasma MDMA measured).

checks.anchor: key_findings[6] (Introduction: sociability and reduced defensiveness cited as a motivator, citing Sumnall et al. 2006)
checks.note: Confirmed in the Introduction's 1st paragraph on p. 73 (Sumnall et al. 2006) and 3rd paragraph on p. 74 (doses of 1 to 2 mg/kg increase extroversion, friendliness, sociability, talkativeness and closeness, with some studies failing to observe these effects).

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[0] (the abstract's sociability-against-placebo claim against the paper's own post hoc threshold)
checks.note: Confirmed. The abstract on p. 73 says 1.5 mg/kg increased self-reported sociability compared with 0.75 mg/kg and placebo; the Results on p. 77 call the placebo contrast marginal; Table 3 (p. 78) prints t(8) 2.5 with p=0.04 and no asterisk, against a stated post hoc threshold of p<0.01; the Figure 2 legend (p. 78) marks it as a marginal difference.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[1] (the abstract's amygdala claim against the corrected p of .052)
checks.note: Confirmed on all three pages, including the phrase on p. 77 describing the corrected result as significant at p=0.052 and the statement on p. 81 that the findings should be regarded as preliminary.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[2] (POMS friendliness: effect size above .23 asserted, statistic not printed)
checks.note: Confirmed on p. 77 (the effect size of the main effect of drug is called large, above 0.23, so the absence of significance may be due to sample size) and in Table 3 on p. 78, which prints only F(2,16)=1.3 for the drug-by-time row. No main-effect statistic for friendliness appears anywhere in the article.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[3] (the 'feel drug' spreads printed as SDs behave like standard errors)
checks.note: Confirmed, and the version of record strengthens it: Table 3's column heading is 'Mean (SD)', but its own footnotes c and d state that the emotion-recognition accuracy and reaction-time values are presented with standard error. The table therefore mixes standard deviations and standard errors under one heading, which the card does not say.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[4] (collected subjective measures not reported)
checks.note: Confirmed: p. 75 lists the four Drug Effects Questionnaire items, the seven visual analogue items and the eight POMS subscales, and names sociability and friendliness as the outcome measures chosen on the basis of the hypotheses; p. 77 reports only those plus 'feel drug', with unwanted effects covered by one sentence.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[5] (ascending dose order confounded with session order)
checks.note: Confirmed: the ascending order on p. 74, the safety reason and the absence of a session-order effect on pp. 81-82. The article reports the absence of an order effect in words only, with no statistic, as the card says.

checks.anchor: analysis.effect_sizes and outcomes.multiplicity_correction: the effects table is called 'Table 2'
checks.note: Disagreement. In the version of record the effects table is Table 3 (p. 78). Table 1 (ecstasy and recent drug use) and Table 2 (lifetime drug use) are on p. 77 and Table 4 (whole-brain clusters) is on p. 80. Reader 709 corrected this in key_findings and reporting_issues on 2026-11-15, but these two fields still say Table 2. The editors' count of 11 rows is right for Table 3.

checks.anchor: design_detail: 'viewed angry, fearful, happy and neutral faces'
checks.note: Disagreement, already logged by reader 709 and still in the card. Each run presented six blocks of faces (happy, neutral, angry, fearful, disgusted and sad) plus a block of radios and seven fixation blocks, fourteen 20-second blocks per run, four runs a session, 18 minutes 40 seconds in all (p. 75; Fig. 1, p. 76); the disgusted and sad blocks were not used in the analyses. Four kinds were analysed, six were shown. The article does not say how long each face was on screen.

checks.anchor: design_detail and comparison.matching: sessions 'on average 10.7 days, SD 7.2'
checks.note: Disagreement of labelling. The article prints 'an average of 10.72 (±7.15) days apart' and does not say whether ±7.15 is a standard deviation or a standard error, so the card's 'SD 7.2' is an assumption.

checks.anchor: outcomes.assessor_blinding: "a 'feel drug' rating averaging 92 of 100"
checks.note: Disagreement of inference. The article gives only the end labels of the visual analogue scales (p. 75) and never states their length, so 'of 100' is an assumption; Table 3 (p. 78) gives 91.8 as the mean peak change from baseline, not a rating on a stated scale.

checks.anchor: funding.funder
checks.note: Agrees in substance. The Acknowledgements on p. 82 print 'National Institute of Drug Abuse (DA02812)'; the card writes the agency's correct name, National Institute on Drug Abuse, with the same grant number. The line 'Disclosures/conflict of interest None' is also on p. 82, as the card says.

checks.anchor: verification.source_read (PMC author manuscript PMC3328967)
checks.note: No disagreement of content was found between the manuscript the card was written from and the version of record, and the printed pages reader 709 assigned all hold. The field can now name the PDF of record as well.

checks.anchor: verification.disagreements: the nine items reader 709 recorded as 'not yet in the card'
checks.note: Checked against the version of record and still absent from the card. Table 4 (p. 80) verified in detail: at p<0.001 uncorrected with a minimum cluster of 80 mm3 the main effect of drug on the angry-against-neutral contrast appears in 21 rows, of which 20 lie outside the a priori regions (Z 3.35 to 4.33, 88 to 848 mm3), the left amygdala row being the a priori one at Z 2.91 and 80 mm3; one cluster for fearful faces; two for happy faces, of which one is the ventral striatum (Z 2.93, 240 mm3); four for the motor-visual contrast. Also verified: the extracted-signal tests (left amygdala F(2,16)=7.24, p<0.01, t(8)=3.34 and 2.44; ventral striatum F(2,16)=8.41, p<0.005, t(8)=5.51 and 2.44) on pp. 77-78; the authors' remark on p. 80 that the ventral striatum effect at 0.75 mg/kg came without any change in sociability ratings; the Gamma et al. 2000 blood-flow caveat on p. 81; the imaging start times 80.8 (±6.6), 82.1 (±12.6) and 91.4 (±10.5) minutes on p. 75; and the reaction-time unit printed in Table 3 as microseconds (p. 78), which cannot be right for values near 1,300 and is presumably milliseconds. The cluster sizes in the Figure 3 and 4 legends (280 mm3 and 1,520 mm3) are not inconsistent with Table 4: the figures show t contrasts, the table the ANOVA main effect.

checks.anchor: key_findings[0] (only four substances; stimulants only inside a composite covariate)
checks.note: Confirmed: the title and abstract on p. 120 name nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine only; section 2.3.1 on p. 121 defines the four exposures; the footnote to Table 2 on p. 124 lists the ten AUDADIS-IV classes, stimulants among them, that make up the composite substance use disorder covariate, with the substance of interest excluded. Nothing in the version of record reports an amphetamine or methamphetamine estimate.

checks.anchor: key_findings[1] (lifetime cumulative probability 67.5 / 22.7 / 20.9 / 8.9 per cent, no intervals)
checks.note: Confirmed in the abstract (p. 120) and in Results 3.3, 1st paragraph (p. 122); no confidence interval is given with any of them. Figure 1, which the card's locator names, is printed on p. 125, not beside the text.

checks.anchor: key_findings[2] (decade 15.6 / 14.8 / 11.0 / 5.9 per cent; first year about 2 per cent and 7.1 per cent for cocaine)
checks.note: Confirmed word for word in Results 3.3, 1st paragraph. The same decade figures are repeated in the Discussion on p. 125 beside the National Comorbidity Survey comparison.

checks.anchor: key_findings[3] (median time to dependence about 27, 13, 5 and 4 years)
checks.note: Confirmed in the abstract (p. 120) and Results 3.3 (p. 122); Figure 1 is on p. 125.

checks.anchor: key_findings[4] (cocaine racial and ethnic differences, 35.9 against 16.8 per cent, log rank 30.40; adjusted hazard ratio 3.45, 2.2 to 5.3)
checks.note: Confirmed: section 3.3.4 on p. 122 gives 16.8, 35.9, 20.5, 20.3 and 22.5 per cent with log rank 30.40, p<0.01, and the median times of about 2, 3, 4, 5 and 4 years by group; Table 4 on p. 127 gives 3.45 (2.2-5.3) for Black against White people who used cocaine.

checks.anchor: key_findings[5] (nicotine 85.1 against 64.1 per cent, log rank 41.53; alcohol 16.9 to 29.0; cannabis 8.2 to 15.9)
checks.note: Confirmed in sections 3.3.1 to 3.3.3, with log rank 41.53 (nicotine), 47.16 (alcohol) and 17.57 (cannabis), all p<0.01.

checks.anchor: key_findings[6] (psychiatric comorbidity hazard ratios across substances)
checks.note: Confirmed in Table 4: mood disorder 1.62, 2.29, 2.69, 2.58; personality disorder 1.42, 1.64, 2.3, 1.99; anxiety disorder 1.96, 1.98, 2.31 with no cocaine entry.

checks.anchor: key_findings[7] (dependence on another substance predicted transition)
checks.note: Confirmed in Table 4: cannabis dependence predicting cocaine dependence 3.84 (1.8-8.2); cocaine dependence predicting cannabis dependence 4.14 (2.3-7.6); alcohol dependence predicting nicotine 2.35, cannabis 2.55 and cocaine 2.56.

checks.anchor: key_findings[8] (early onset: unadjusted 1.29 / 2.51 / 2.47 / 1.65, adjusted 1.13 / none / 0.63 / 0.34)
checks.note: Confirmed: Table 3 on p. 126 gives the unadjusted hazard ratios 1.29 (1.2-1.4), 2.51 (2.3-2.7), 2.47 (2.0-3.1) and 1.65 (0.9-3.0); Table 4 on p. 127 gives 1.13 (1.1-1.2) for nicotine, 0.63 (0.5-0.9) for cannabis and 0.34 (0.1-0.9) for cocaine, with no alcohol entry; section 3.4.2 runs from p. 123 to p. 125 and the Discussion paragraph the card cites, which reads the reversal as early onset marking concomitant comorbidity, is on p. 128. The note's cell of 51 people who used cocaine before age 14 is in Table 2 on p. 124.

checks.anchor: key_findings[9] (co-occurring substance use disorders: editors' 51 / 31 / 81 / 93 per cent against the discussion's one third, half, more than 80 and 90 per cent)
checks.note: Confirmed: Table 2 on p. 124 gives 8131 of 16053, 8962 of 29160, 5967 of 7409 and 2098 of 2263 (editors' arithmetic: 50.7, 30.7, 80.5 and 92.7 per cent), and the Discussion sentence naming one third, half, more than 80 per cent and 90 per cent is on p. 127, not on the page of the table.

checks.anchor: key_findings[10] (43,093 at Wave 1, 34,653 at Wave 2, subsamples 15,918 / 28,907 / 7,389 / 2,259)
checks.note: Confirmed: section 2.1 on p. 121 gives 43,093 and 34,653 and the Wave 2 eligibility counts (not deceased n=1403, deported or mentally or physically impaired n=781, on active military duty n=950); the four subsample sizes are on p. 121 and in the abstract on p. 120. The reliability figures the card cites are also on p. 121: kappa 0.54 to 0.91 for substance use disorder diagnoses and 0.40 to 0.77 for psychiatric diagnoses.

checks.anchor: key_findings[11] (limitations stated by the authors)
checks.note: Confirmed: the paragraph beginning 'The present findings should be interpreted in light of common limitations' lists all five in the card's order (self-report not confirmed objectively; recall bias growing with the interval and with drug-related cognitive impairment; intermittent rather than continuous use making the elapsed time inexact; exclusion of institutionalized people, who have a higher probability of a dependence diagnosis; income not modellable as a time-dependent covariate).

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[0] (Table 1 row totals differ from the stated subsample sizes by 135, 253, 20 and 4)
checks.note: Confirmed on p. 123: every stratification of Table 1 sums to 16,053, 29,160, 7,409 and 2,263 against headings of 15,918, 28,907, 7,389 and 2,259. The card can be strengthened: the same mismatch is inside Table 2 on p. 124, whose rows also sum to 16,053, 29,160, 7,409 and 2,263 under the same headings, so the discrepancy is not confined to Table 1.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[1] (Table 2: psychiatric-disorder counts identical to mood-disorder counts, percentages different)
checks.note: Confirmed exactly: the 'no' rows give 11458 at 27.4 per cent for any psychiatric disorder and 11458 at 44.5 per cent for any mood disorder (nicotine), and 4573 at 5.1 per cent against 4573 at 17.7 per cent (cannabis); the 'yes' rows repeat the pattern (4595 at 58.0 and 53.0 per cent; 2836 at 31.0 and 32.5 per cent). The two rows cannot both be right.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[2] (dependence cases in Tables 3 and 4 fewer than the lifetime diagnoses in Table 2)
checks.note: Confirmed: Table 2 on p. 124 gives 7473, 4869, 564 and 398 lifetime dependence diagnoses; Tables 3 (p. 126) and 4 (p. 127) are headed N = 7320, 4822, 529 and 376. The shortfall is not explained anywhere in the version of record.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[3] (overall median latency longer than the median for White people, the largest group)
checks.note: Confirmed: overall 13 years for alcohol and 4 for cocaine (section 3.3), against about 8 years for White people who used alcohol (3.3.2) and about 2 years for White people who used cocaine (3.3.4). The same pattern holds for nicotine, which the card does not mention: 27 years overall against about 23 for White, 26 for Hispanic, 24 for American Indian or Alaska Native and 18 for Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander people, with only Black people at 30 years above the overall figure.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[4] (section 3.1 lists alcohol twice where cocaine is meant)
checks.note: Confirmed in the first sentence of section 3.1.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[5] (Table 1 prints an income cell as '44.o')
checks.note: Confirmed in the nicotine column, individual income 70,000 dollars or more. Two further small print slips of the same kind, not on the card: Table 1 prints 4.87 for cocaine use among people aged 45 and over and Table 2 prints 9.54 for the cocaine anxiety-disorder row, where every other percentage in both tables carries one decimal.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[6] (no confidence intervals for any cumulative transition probability)
checks.note: Confirmed: none is given in the abstract, in Results 3.3 and 3.3.1 to 3.3.4, or in the Discussion. Section 2.4 on p. 121 says 95 per cent intervals were computed for the weighted frequencies used to characterise the sample, not for the survival estimates.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[7] (stepwise selection leaves covariates out of some columns of Table 4)
checks.note: Confirmed: section 2.4 on p. 121 states that stepwise model selection based on the likelihood-ratio test was used; in Table 4 on p. 127 the cocaine column has no gender and no age-group entry, the cannabis column no marital status, and the non-selected estimates are not shown.

checks.anchor: reporting_issues[8] ('The PMC author manuscript carries no funding statement, acknowledgements or conflict-of-interest declaration')
checks.note: Disagreement, and the one that matters. The version of record has all three on p. 128. Role of funding source: NIH grants DA019606, DA020783, DA023200, DA023973, MH076051, MH082773 and CA133050 (Dr Blanco) and AA014223, DA018652 and AA018111 (Dr Hasin), a grant from the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention (Dr Blanco), and the New York State Psychiatric Institute (Drs Blanco and Hasin), with a statement that none of these had any further role in the design, the collection, analysis and interpretation of data, the writing of the report or the decision to submit. Contributors: Blanco designed the study, Lopez-Quintero managed the literature searches and wrote the first draft, Wang did the statistical analyses, and all authors approved the final manuscript. Conflict of interest: None. The issue should be withdrawn and the funding field rewritten from p. 128.

checks.anchor: funding.funder, funding.declared_conflicts, funding.affiliations_note
checks.note: Same disagreement at field level: 'Not reported in the PMC author manuscript' and 'Not reported in this version of the article' are both superseded by the version of record. The card's observation that an author of the survey's custodian agency is among the authors still stands, but the printed statement says the funders had no further role in the work.

checks.anchor: analysis.selective_reporting and outcomes (supplementary tables not read)
checks.note: Confirmed: section 3.2 on p. 122 says the characteristics of the people who developed dependence are in supplementary tables in the online version, and Appendix A on p. 128 gives the link. Those tables were not among the files for this round and were not read.

checks.anchor: every anchor's page field (all are recorded as 'PMC HTML')
checks.note: No anchor was mislocated. The printed pages for the card's anchors, in card order, are: key findings 120/121/124, 120+122+125, 122, 120+122+125, 122+127, 122, 127, 127, 123-125+126+127+128, 124+127, 120+121, 128; reporting issues 121+123+124, 124, 124+126+127, 122, 122, 123, 120+122+125, 121+127, 128. The card may be re-anchored to these printed pages.
